Shortly after confirming its opening date for this coming December, the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi announced that Valerie Hillings will serve as the museum's inaugural director. Hillings returns to the Guggenheim's United Arab Emirates outpost after having previously served as its associate director of curatorial affairs from 2009 to 2018.

Hillings has led the North Carolina Museum of Art (NCMA) in Raleigh for the last eight years. Her tenure was marked by acquisitions for the "People's Collection" — a reinterpretation of the museum's holdings through the lens of public accessibility. Under her leadership, NCMA's collection strategy emphasized acquiring work by women, LGBTQIA+, minority, and local artists.

While strategic, Hillings's appointment at the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi stokes the ongoing controversy surrounding the exploitation and dire forced labor conditions for the migrant construction workers who built out the museum, alongside the Louvre Abu Dhabi and the New York University campus, on Saadiyat Island.

The labor conditions have sparked multiple protest interventions and calls to boycott the Guggenheim Foundation over the last 15 years.

Before joining the NCMA, Hillings worked for the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation from 2004 to 2018. She began on the curatorial team at the Guggenheim Museum in Manhattan, co-organizing and curating topical and collections-based exhibitions onsite and internationally. In 2009, two years before site work for the Frank Gehry-designed building began, Hilling was tapped to develop the collection for the Abu Dhabi outpost in partnership with the city's Department of Culture and Tourism.

The growing collection and forthcoming exhibitions center output and art movements from 1960 onward that “reflect and advance Abu Dhabi’s role as a catalyst for creative production and innovation in the arts,” per a press release from the Guggenheim Foundation.

]]><![CDATA[Kimsooja Comes Full Circle]]>https://hyperallergic.com/kimsooja-comes-full-circle/6a722a41a42e78000150e32bTue, 04 Aug 2026 19:14:46 GMT

TORONTO — Kimsooja held her first North American solo exhibition, Soo-ja Kim: A Laundry Field/Sewing into Walking, Looking into Sewing, nearly 30 years ago. Organized at the Oakville Galleries, a contemporary art museum in an affluent Lake Ontario town approximately 22 miles (~35.4 km) west of Toronto, the artist had the Centennial Gallery walls painted black and hung dozens of colorful, used Korean bedcovers from clotheslines.

“There is a swirling energy from the overhead fans as the bedcovers create alleyways for the viewer to walk through or between,” writes Oakville Galleries Curator of Contemporary Art Marnie Fleming in the exhibition catalog. “Wind generated movement becomes animation as Kim makes the bed covers’ intimate relationship with women’s lives, as well as their role in divisive labour, instructively visible.”

Today — many international exhibitions, commissions, and biennial and triennial representations later — she returns to Toronto with Kimsooja: Dimensions of a Needle at the Museum of Contemporary Art Toronto (MOCA). The taut survey of works from the past 20 years succinctly captures her methodical experiments with video performance, architectural installation, and ceramics, not to mention her single-minded focus on the needle as a metaphor for folding and unfolding, memory and displacement. Rooted in the artist’s increasingly immaterial philosophy of “non-doing” and “non-making,” the site-specific installations take over MOCA’s first and third floors, savvily beginning on its main floor with “To Breathe—Mokum” (2025–26), a work that intentionally recalls the clothesline installation of “A Laundry Field.” 

]]><![CDATA[The Day I Pleated With Iris van Herpen]]>https://hyperallergic.com/the-day-i-pleated-with-iris-van-herpen/6a70ec265b2e060001386c50Tue, 04 Aug 2026 18:23:22 GMT

"Hands are like a language," Iris van Herpen says as we pleat a textile together inside the recreated atelier at the center of Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses. “Each pair that joins me in creating this dress will influence the DNA of the garment.” 

A first of its kind, the live installation at the Brooklyn Museum invites visitors to work alongside the Dutch fashion designer in creating a garment that will evolve over the course of the show’s run. 

“I want to share the most beautiful part of my work — the craftsmanship — in a really intimate setting,” van Herpen tells Hyperallergic in an interview. “My atelier is my most sacred space.” 

Based in the Netherlands, she will periodically return to the recreated studio throughout the exhibition, transforming visitors’ pleated textiles into a garment and embroidering fragments of their conversations into it.

]]><![CDATA[10 Art Shows to See in Los Angeles This August]]>https://hyperallergic.com/10-art-shows-to-see-in-los-angeles-this-august/6a72144e5b2e06000139ff7fTue, 04 Aug 2026 17:35:07 GMT

For the dog days of August, we’ve got several shows that turn away from grand artistic gestures toward the intimate, personal, and everyday. Lisson showcases Spencer Finch’s torn-envelope interventions, bits of painted and collaged wonder. Textiles as Monument at the Fowler Museum features three artists who use soft materials to memorialize those excluded from mainstream historical recognition. A show honoring the longstanding, recently demolished Echo Park restaurant Taix tries to capture its eccentric charm as a home for neighborhood regulars and Gen-Z bohemians alike. And a show at Roberts Projects focused on the garment, jewelry, and costume design of the late assemblage art pioneer Betye Saar shines a light on this important but overlooked aspect of her oeuvre.

Let's Get It On: The Wearable Art of Betye Saar 

Roberts Projects, 442 South La Brea Avenue, Hancock Park, Los Angeles
Through August 22

Betye Saar, who passed away last week at the age of 99, was a pioneering figure in LA assemblage, crafting astute juxtapositions of found objects that celebrated Black and female representation with wit, humor, and biting social critique. Let’s Get it On focuses on a lesser-known part of her practice: her costume design. The show includes more than 200 garments, photographs, and drawings spanning the 1950s through the 1970s. Among them are her costume designs for productions at the Inner City Cultural Center, a multicultural performing arts space formed after the 1965 Watts Rebellion, as well as clothes she made for her daughters to wear at the Renaissance Pleasure Faire at the Paramount Ranch in the late ’60s and early ’70s. Based heavily on archival research, the exhibition adds a crucial puzzle piece to Saar’s extensive legacy.

]]><![CDATA[AI Is the New Book Burning]]>https://hyperallergic.com/ai-is-the-new-book-burning/6a70f2975b2e060001386e4fTue, 04 Aug 2026 10:00:04 GMTJust when we thought tech companies couldn’t get more odious, they took a page from the long, tyrannical tradition of book burning. Author and bibliophile Ed Simon opines today about the horrific revelation that Anthropic scanned and then shredded out-of-print books to train its large language models, a shameless act of artistic plunder aimed at gutting our humanity. Read and share, and take this as a sign to support your local library while you’re at it.

Meanwhile, artists continue to offer glimmers of hope in unexpected places. Case in point: psychedelic pickleball courts in Pittsburgh (say that five times fast). A co-founder of the experimental collective Hilma’s Ghost and proponent of public art, Sharmistha Ray designed vivid murals in their signature geometric style to bring one of the city’s recreational spaces to life. Say what you want about pickleball, but it gets the people going.

More today, including a tribute to beloved dealer and Lubov gallerist Francisco Correa Cordero, who passed away on Sunday at age 37.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity

The recent revelation about Anthropic’s systematic digitization and destruction of out-of-print books portends a rapacious future, one where soulless LLMs swell while the shelves starve. | Ed Simon

I grew up in the 60's and 70's in San Francisco where all library racks were packed tight and high. Cozy corners everywhere to stroll through random new finds I could discover no other way. Even as late as 2000 in Fremont, California their main Library was packed tight and high. But since, every library I have entered has been de-libraried. From my questioning and listening, the new government management mentality has been to turn libraries, and indeed any similar public service facility, into "community centers" with programs and gimmicks to make government appear to be serving public desires. But all one has to do is look at the racks and the "program promotion" campaigns to see the actual intent: to de-intellectualize and spectacularize the public sphere. A form of happy-washing cultural wipe-out.

Francisco Correa Cordero, the founder of the downtown New York gallery Lubov, died on Sunday, August 2, at the age of 37. The news of his passing was announced by the gallery’s Instagram account today, August 3. 

The cause of death was not listed, but the gallery said in its statement that he passed away "surrounded by what he loved the most — his chosen family, laughter and so much love."

]]><![CDATA[Eric Carle Museum Workers Push for Union Vote]]>https://hyperallergic.com/eric-carle-museum-workers-push-for-union-vote/6a70ba095b2e060001385382Mon, 03 Aug 2026 21:01:21 GMT

Brown bear, brown bear, what do you see? The Eric Carle Museum staff have started unionizing. Workers announced the news on Instagram on August 3, amid staff allegations of understaffing, a lack of promotions, and poor workplace conditions at the Massachusetts museum established by the beloved children's book author and illustrator.

According to their post, employees filed for a full-time and part-time staff election with the National Labor Relations Board. "We call upon Museum leadership not to interfere with or delay a union vote," the post reads. Under representation from the United Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2110, the group demanded that as many staff as possible be allowed to vote in the election, given they fit the eligibility criteria.

Carle, the late children's book artist best known for The Very Hungry Caterpillar (1969) and his collaboration with Bill Martin Jr. on Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See? (1967), founded the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in November 2002 with his wife, Barbara Carle. In the 23 years since its opening, the museum has welcomed more than a million visitors to Amherst, Massachusetts, to see the author's illustrations and iconic tissue paper collages.

However, a litany of recent allegations have pushed museum staff to the point of unionizing.

Pickleball aficionados in downtown Pittsburgh get to enjoy an art experience as they play thanks to artist Sharmistha Ray's vibrant floor murals.

The artist's new "Geometry of Play" installation invites the public to step into — and onto — the vibrant surfaces, pickleball paddle in hand.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Two alumni from the Interlochen Center for the Arts in Michigan have come forward with previously unreported abuse allegations against Jeffrey Epstein while he was a benefactor of the school.

The alumni's allegations against the financier, which include claims of sexual misconduct and assault, emerged during a two-year external investigation into a history of abuse at the arts boarding school and summer camp.

In addition to the new accounts about Epstein, the investigation culminated in a 97-page report in which dozens of alumni made abuse allegations against 47 adults affiliated with the school between the 1950s and the 2010s.

]]><![CDATA[Ellen Pau’s Elegy to a Vanishing Hong Kong]]>https://hyperallergic.com/ellen-paus-elegy-to-a-vanishing-hong-kong/6a70c69c5b2e060001385b63Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:56:06 GMT

Drops of water trickle down a plain white wall under a heavenly light in Ellen Pau’s 1988 video installation “She Moves 她去.” Flanked by soft white veils and a nostalgic, wooden armchair, the work introduces water as a central motif in Pau’s long-standing interest in Hong Kong as a city in constant transition, moving through cycles of lost and found.

Ellen Pau: She Moves at SculptureCenter, curated by Freya Chou, is the first United States survey exhibition of the woman widely regarded as Hong Kong’s video art pioneer. Across 15 videos and installations spanning the late 1980s to the present, water reappears in various forms: a crying wall, swimmers diving into Victoria Harbour, the scent of tear gas. Its changing states, from melting ice to evaporating mist, become a metaphor for Hong Kong herself — “always on the verge of disappearing,” as late cultural theorist Ackbar Abbas puts it — leaving little time for reflection before new changes arrive.

The city’s rapid transformation is reflected in the afterlife of “She Moves.” Over the years, the work has been transferred across formats — NTSC to PAL, VHS to DVD — remastered, and, most recently, restored with AI. With each iteration, something is lost, and something new is layered in. That state of flux is mirrored by the installation, an intimate space that invites viewers to take a seat, temporarily occupying the position of an absent subject. Who is the “she” in the title? Could it be Pau herself, who once rested in that very chair; the woman in a floral dress, who appears briefly on screen; the visitors who enter and exit the space; or even Hong Kong herself?

Upon entering the underground, labyrinthine corridor, visitors encounter a work from Pau’s ongoing, multisensory Fl0ra Zero series (2016–ongoing), “Where Have All the Flowers Gone 冇花 冇假” (2026). It starts with burnt candles attached to the wall, collected by Pau and her friends over the years from the June 4 vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. On the opposite side, strips of film negatives hang from a rack, bearing ghostly silhouettes of these candles, preserving the outline of what once was. Translated into photographic images, the candles’ shifting forms draw a parallel to the making and preservation of historical records — just as light fixes a passing moment onto film, archives preserve ephemeral experiences as material records that outlast their original time. Close to the floor lie flesh-like lumps of melted wax, remnants of “Spectre of the Will” (2019), a single-channel video installation in which an infrared camera captured visitors standing before a heated wall, translating their body temperature into live heat maps. The surrounding wax slowly melted in response to the increasing energy, recalling the blood, sweat, and lives spent in collective resistance. 

The smell of burnt bark and chemicals fills the air — intermittently released into the corridor is “Sublime,” a fragrance developed by Pau with scent specialist Xavier Tseng to recreate the smell of tear gas. Visitors may find their eyes watering as they move through the space, momentarily inhabiting the danger and vulnerability of participating in public protests. It’s a direct reference to recent protests in Hong Kong, where tear gas deployed by the police against protesters became sensory evidence of state violence and the suppression of civic expression. 

Near the end of the tunnel, a holographic flame burns atop a bloodstained-looking structure resembling the torch of the Goddess of Democracy, a symbol during the Tiananmen Square protests. As viewers approach the work, motion sensors activate, switching the video feed from crackling fire to footage of burning film strips. On one hand, the work references the traditional Chinese practice of burning offerings for the dead; on the other, it comments on the altering and erasure of public records, both elegy and critique. 

Since the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration set the terms for Hong Kong’s 1997 handover, questions around identity and autonomy have loomed over the consciousness of every local. In “She Moves,” Vera Lynn’s 1939 wartime anthem “We’ll Meet Again” plays, alluding to recent protests and migration waves in Hong Kong that split families and communities. Originally written for lovers separated by war, its promise of reunion captures the hope that, as Pau put it in her recent artist talk at the Asia Art Archives in New York, Hong Kongers will all meet again on a bright sunny day.

Ellen Pau: She Moves continues at SculptureCenter (44-19 Purves Street, Long Island City, Queens) through August 16. The exhibition was curated by Freya Chou.

Editor's note 8/4/26 12:58pm: A previous version of this article stated that Rain Chan designed the exhibition; he designed part of it. It also stated that the chair in Ellen Pau's installation "She Moves" (1988) was once in her home.

]]><![CDATA[AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity]]>https://hyperallergic.com/ai-companies-are-pulping-our-humanity/6a70c2705b2e06000138599eMon, 03 Aug 2026 17:52:37 GMT

After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile. And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that.

In a sobering report by Frank Landymore in Futurism, published last Saturday, explains that Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly trained on their own slop, creating a need to train them on pre-2022 writing that is uncontaminated by AI itself — that’s the particular sales pitch made by ISBNdb, a company supplying bulk orders of books to tech companies — with purchases of between one thousand and one million volumes at a time. A “hydraulic powered cutting machine” slices off book spines and removes the pages, which are scanned and digitized before being pulped. This process of “destructive scanning” is a way to elude copyright regulations through a legal loophole, with the result being that “an AI company could be destroying some of the few remaining copies that can be found” of these books.

The destruction of books, as Servetus’s case demonstrates, is hardly a historical rarity. Nor is the pulping of books for non-ideological reasons uncommon, as publishers are responsible for destroying nearly 25% of works released each year, almost always because they didn’t sell.

Rather, what the recent revelation portends is unique and terrifying: the rapacious, cannibalistic devouring of culture so as to feed the very technology meant to replace the human. The indifference of the LLM is chilling in its own way; one imagines that if a copy of Servetus’s book fell beneath the lifeless eye of the digitizer, it would simply upload all of those theological arguments into the hungry maw of the machine, where it would only serve as fodder for the advanced plagiarism device which is artificial intelligence.

“We see a future where intelligence is a utility,” said OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, “and people buy it from us on a meter.”

This is a future where technocracy has accomplished its war against the sacred materiality and artistry of the book itself, where everything is reduced to so much predictive binary. It’s an act of literal erasure for which George Orwell’s cliched warning that “who controls the past controls the future” is restored to its original impact. LLMs swell while the shelves starve, the result being an act of libricide, of corporate indifference to the obliteration of culture, ideas, and humanity itself.

]]><![CDATA[Betye Saar, Simone Forti, Walter Benjamin]]>https://hyperallergic.com/betye-saar-simone-forti-walter-benjamin/6a6cbd7075d29f00013c3390Sat, 01 Aug 2026 10:00:32 GMTHow many days of your life have been ruined because of someone else's fragile ego? How many times have so-called "friends" shamelessly stolen your ideas? In this month's Art Problems column, Paddy Johnson tackles an uncomfortable question: Why are there so many toxic people in the art world? Read her tips on how to protect yourself from insecure peers and bad-faith actors. Hope it helps. 

Speaking of toxic people, President Trump has ordered the installation of content warning signs outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History to alert the public against the institution's alleged leftist bias. 

"No other president has seen fit to vandalize taxpayer-funded museums with a billboard telling people not to go inside, while directing them to more politically 'palatable' — which is to say extreme right-wing — revisions of the historical record," writes Ed Simon in a must-read opinion piece below.

In other stories, this week we said goodbye to two giants: assemblage artist Betye Saar, who died just four days before her 100th birthday, and performance artist Simone Forti, who passed away at 91. We mourn their death while celebrating the massive legacies they've left behind.  

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Madrid Museum Puts Picasso in Dialogue With “African Guernica”

Spanning over 25-feet wide and 11-feet high, Pablo Picasso’s painting “Guernica” (1937) is as monumental in size as it is in cultural significance. Its startling depiction of state brutality against civilians has made it an emblem of post-war Spanish identity, and its cry against violence has resonated with besieged people worldwide — from Vietnam to Gaza — throughout the past nine decades.

A new annual exhibition series at the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid, which has served as the canonical work’s permanent home since 1992, places “Guernica” in dialogue with other artworks. The new program, titled History Doesn’t Repeat Itself, but It Does Rhyme, partly aims to revisit the universal political impulses behind the anti-war painting — but its first iteration also exposes race as an urgent issue for contemporary art institutions in Spain. | Agnish Ray

In a 2013 essay, author Barrett Swanson asked, “At what point does the aesthetic excellence of the photograph eclipse the depicted event, or, worse, distract the viewer from inquiring into what happened?” With the synchronous explosion of digital news content and unremitting global calamity, it’s a question that strongly resonates today, particularly with photography of protest and social movements. If these images overtly flatter the protestor, they can be accused of fueling performative activism and pulling attention away from the crisis at hand; if they are too beautiful, they might conceal the real risk of violence from the state. Still, if they are too graphic, they can rob the subjects of their dignity, making a cheap spectacle of dissidence.

These are tensions of which photographer-activist Misan Harriman, who has rapidly made a name for himself documenting protests since the summer of 2020, is no doubt keenly aware.

Harriman is the subject of Andy Mundy-Castle’s new documentary Shoot the People, which follows the 48-year-old Nigerian-born Brit as he chronicles activist movements across three continents. While Harriman's evolution from an amateur photographer to the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of Vogue's September edition is impressive, more exigent is his artful representation of protests, especially (though not exclusively) those in which primarily Black and Brown people are filling the streets.
